scene.testo: Seventeen written questions. One officer. One prisoner. Question fifteen asked what historians still want to know. When did you realize the Allies could no longer be held on the Normandy beachhead? Give a date, or a number of divisions.
The prisoner did not write a number of divisions. He did not write a month, or a vague season. He wrote one precise day. It was not June sixth. It was a day many Americans have never heard of.

The summer of 1945. A luxury hotel in Luxembourg, seized by the United States Army and turned into a prison. Inside it, American Army historians handed a captured German general a questionnaire about Normandy.

The general was Alfred Jodl. For years he had run operations for the German armed forces high command. Three months earlier, he had signed Germany's surrender. Now he was answering questions in writing.

Jodl was not a field commander. He was a staff planner. From August 1939, he directed operations for the high command, working a few doors from Hitler through every campaign, from Norway and France to the Soviet Union.

On May seventh, 1945, in a red brick schoolhouse in Reims, Jodl signed Germany's unconditional surrender before Eisenhower's staff. By summer he was confined at Mondorf, a former spa hotel the Allies called Ashcan.

There, he wrote his answers by hand and signed them on August second, 1945. His tone was calm and factual. The voice of a professional staff officer. Read in order, his pages show a man watching the western front come apart.

The Americans began with German strategy. In the summer of 1944, Field Marshal Rommel proposed a radical step. Pull the German line back south of Caen. Let the Allies advance onto open ground. Then crush their flank with massed armor.

Jodl opposed the idea, and Hitler agreed with him. In open country, Jodl explained, the enemy could use his air superiority and his mobility. Once the line broke, Germany could no longer hold France. So every hedgerow had to be defended.

Hermann Goering floated another idea. Drop German paratroopers behind Allied lines near Bayeux. Jodl rejected that too. Germany, he wrote, no longer had trained paratroopers, and transport aircraft could never get through the Allied front.

Then the Americans asked why the Germans expected the main Allied attack from the British, around Caen. Jodl's answer was blunt. We considered the British stronger and more experienced in combat, and so more dangerous than the Americans.

The British sector also lay on the shortest road to Paris. So Germany massed its tanks there. And there they stayed, week after week, holding off the British in some of the fiercest fighting of the campaign.

Asked whether he had ever felt confident of holding the beachhead, Jodl admitted that his early hopes faded. Enemy reinforcements, he wrote, were flowing far faster than ours. Week after week, he was losing hope.

On July twentieth, Jodl's own war almost ended differently. He stood at the map table in Hitler's East Prussian headquarters when Colonel von Stauffenberg's briefcase bomb exploded. Jodl suffered a head wound, but he survived.
Five days later, in Normandy, the day he would name arrived. Here is question fifteen, exactly as the Americans put it. When did you think you would no longer be able to hold the beachhead?

And here is Jodl's reply, word for word. Since July twenty-fifth, when the violent attacks by the Americans on the western flank began as well, I had serious doubts about our ability to hold the beachhead at all.

His day was July twenty-fifth, 1944. Not D-Day. Not the battles around Caen. It was the morning the Americans launched Operation Cobra, General Omar Bradley's plan to punch a hole through the hedgerows west of Saint-Lo.
Instead of attacking along the whole front, Bradley picked a narrow stretch of road, pulled his men back from it, and asked heavy bombers to flatten a zone one mile deep and five miles wide.

The first attempt, on July twenty-fourth, went wrong. Clouds covered the target, the recall order came late, and some bombs fell short on American troops, killing 25 soldiers. On the other side, the Germans believed they had held.

General Fritz Bayerlein, commanding the elite Panzer Lehr Division, believed his men had just beaten back a major American attack. Expecting more American artillery, he pulled his forward troops south of the road, straight into the bombing zone.

At 9:38 the next morning, the sky was clear and the bombers returned. More than 1,500 American heavy bombers, followed by hundreds of medium bombers and fighter-bombers, dropped over 4,000 tons of bombs on that narrow strip of Normandy.
Bayerlein lived to describe it. By noon, he said, the whole area looked like the surface of the moon, bomb craters joined rim to rim. Tanks were overturned and buried. Communication lines were cut.
The official Air Force history records an estimate that seventy percent of his men were out of action, killed, wounded, or stunned senseless. And again, bombs fell short on American lines.

More than 100 American soldiers were killed, among them Lieutenant General Lesley McNair, the highest ranking American officer killed in the European war. American commanders feared the attack had stalled.

In fact, as the official Army history put it, the attack had succeeded beyond anyone's expectations. The Germans knew it better than the Americans. That evening, Field Marshal von Kluge, the German commander in the West, acknowledged it.

Two days later, Bayerlein reported his Panzer Lehr Division annihilated. And what makes Jodl's questionnaire so revealing is what came next. The Americans asked whether he had expected the blow, and whether he had noticed strong American forces gathering west of Saint-Lo.

Jodl wrote that he could not recall receiving a precise report of particularly strong American forces preparing west of Saint-Lo. When Cobra began, seven of the ten German armored divisions in Normandy were still around Caen, facing the British.

The decisive blow came where Hitler's chief planner was not looking. Then the Americans asked how many divisions he had sent from Brittany to stop the breakthrough at Avranches. His answer was none. We were too weak in Brittany by then.

On July thirtieth, American tanks entered Avranches and found its bridges intact. General Patton's Third Army poured through the gap into open French countryside. It was exactly the war of movement and air power Jodl had warned would destroy them.

Within three weeks, German armies in Normandy were trapped and crushed in the Falaise pocket. On August twenty-fifth, Paris was free. Jodl had feared that once the line broke, France could not be held. He was right.
Jodl's signed pages went into the files of the United States Army, and he went to a cell at Nuremberg. The tribunal convicted him on all four counts of the indictment.

On October sixteenth, 1946, Alfred Jodl was hanged, in the same night as Ribbentrop and Keitel. The staff officer who signed Germany's surrender at Reims had already signed one more page for the Americans.

On it, he recorded the day he stopped believing Normandy could be held, and the army that took it from him. Jodl named July twenty-fifth. But seven weeks earlier, on the morning of June sixth, Germany had its best chance.

That day, Germany had its best chance to throw the invasion back into the sea. And when the Americans asked Field Marshal von Rundstedt why D-Day succeeded, he answered with two words, which he repeated three times.
That story is on your screen now. Subscribe for more of what the men on the other side said, in their own words, and watch that video next.

descrizione:
In the summer of 1945, American Army historians gave captured German General Alfred Jodl a written questionnaire about Normandy. Question fifteen asked when he stopped believing the Allied beachhead could be contained. His answer was not June 6, 1944. It was one specific day.

This documentary follows Jodl's own signed answers, from the strategy debate over Rommel's plan to Operation Cobra, the massive bombing near Saint-Lo, the breakthrough at Avranches, and the collapse of the German front in France.

Source material includes Allied interrogation records, the official US Army history, and Nuremberg records. Subscribe to WWII Testimony for more of what the men on the other side said in their own words.
